paragraphs: Long ago, by the edge of a quiet sea, there lived a poor fisherman and his wife in a small, weathered pigsty near the shore.
Each morning, the fisherman walked to the water with his net and rod, and each evening he returned with whatever the sea was willing to give.
Their life was simple. Their home was small. Though they worked hard, they never had much.
Still, the fisherman was gentle of heart and thankful for what little he had.
One day, as he stood by the shore watching the waves glimmer in the sunlight, his line suddenly pulled deep into the water. He drew it up slowly and found a great fish shining in the light.
To his surprise, the fish spoke.
“Please let me live,” said the fish softly. “I am not a real fish, but an enchanted prince. Put me back into the sea.”
The fisherman did not hesitate.
“A talking fish is no fish for me,” he said kindly. “Swim away in peace.”
And he returned the fish to the water, where it vanished beneath the waves.
That evening, when he told his wife what had happened, she stared at him in disbelief.
“You let an enchanted prince go,” she said, “and you asked for nothing?”
She looked around their poor little pigsty.
“We live so poorly,” she said. “Go back and ask the fish for a small cottage.”
The fisherman did not like the idea, but he loved his wife. So the next day, he returned to the sea.
The water no longer looked clear and bright. It was yellow and green, and the waves rolled slowly.
He stood at the shore and called,
“O man of the sea,
Hearken to me.
My wife Ilsabill
Will have her own will,
And has sent me to beg a boon of thee.”
The fish rose from the water.
“What does your wife wish?” he asked.
“She wishes for a little cottage,” said the fisherman.
“Go home,” said the fish. “She has it already.”
The fisherman returned and found a neat little cottage with flowers in the garden. His wife was pleased.
For a while, they lived happily there.
But soon, Ilsabill sighed. “This cottage is too small. I want a stone castle.”
Uneasily, the fisherman went back to the sea. Now the water was blue and gloomy.
Again the fish listened.
“Go home,” said the fish. “She is standing at a castle gate.”
The fisherman returned to find a great stone castle where the cottage had been. Servants hurried through wide halls, and golden chairs gleamed.
“Now we have enough,” he said softly.
But Ilsabill only nodded.
The next morning, she said, “We must be king of this land.”
Though he protested, the fisherman returned to the sea. The water was dark gray, and the waves curled with foam.
“Go home,” said the fish. “She is king already.”
His wife now sat upon a golden throne, crowned and surrounded by music and soldiers.
Yet she soon said, “I want to be emperor.”
Again the fisherman went. The sea was black and muddy, the wind fierce.
“Go home,” said the fish. “She is emperor.”
Still unsatisfied, Ilsabill declared, “I will be pope.”
The fisherman trembled as he returned once more. The sea was wild with storm, the sky dark.
“Go home,” said the fish. “She is pope.”
Ilsabill now sat upon a throne higher than any tower, wearing three great crowns. Power shone all around her.
But even then, she could not sleep.
At dawn, she said, “I will be lord of the sun and moon.”
The fisherman walked to the sea one final time. A terrible storm raged. Waves rose like mountains, and lightning burned the sky.
“What does your wife want now?” asked the fish.
“She wants to command the sun and moon,” the fisherman whispered.
The fish spoke only once more.
“Go home,” he said. “To your pigsty again.”
When the fisherman returned, the castle was gone. The palace was gone. The crowns were gone.
There stood the old pigsty by the sea.
And inside it was his wife.
And so they lived once more by the shore, with no riches and no power—only the quiet sound of the sea.
And the lesson of a gentle truth:
That wanting more and more can make you lose what you already have.
And that the greatest riches are found in peace.
